doc.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Being a professional hired gun and the A team and Wrecking Crew
summary: Studio players stay professional whatever the music; he describes the competitive session scene, the Wrecking Crew, Nashville's A team and Hank Garland.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: When you went to do a session invariably you’re going to be playing music that you might not like. How do you adjust your attitude towards that.

You just have to be professional. You were hired guns and you were only as good as your last record that you were playing on. So it was very competitive. Everybody wanted to be a studio player and very few get through the keyhole. Especially back then. It’s not so that way — it’s almost a nonexistent art now because the way people make records they very seldom hire studio musicians. In Nashville they do but not like it used to be. It used to be literally three sessions, sometimes four sessions a day, six or seven days a week. We would work all the time. And there was a generation or two ahead of us from the late 50s through the 60s, the Wrecking Crew in LA, every major recording center had one or two rhythm sections. LA it was the Wrecking Crew, which was a loosely knit group of great players, usually three guitars, two keyboardists, electric bass, an upright bass, multiple instrumentalists. And Nashville it was the A team, the historic A team that played on the Owen Bradley/Patsy Cline records and all those things for Chet [Atkins]. But I mean one of the great guitarists back in those days in the 60s was a fellow named Hank Garland. He played on “Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree” and all that kind of stuff, but he did a jazz album called “Jazz Winds from a New Direction” I think. And it was Joe Morello and oh my gosh the great vibraphone player, a young guy back then, but it was jazz players from New York and he cut this great jazz album. They could all play jazz. Chet could play jazz.
